**What this PR does / why we need it**:

This PR implements [KEP 2000 (Graceful Node Shutdown)](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-node/2000-graceful-node-shutdown). 

This PR makes it possible for kubelet to be aware of node shutdown events and gracefully terminate pods during a system shutdown. Refer to the KEP for more details. 

This PR adds a new alpha feature gate in kubelet, `GracefulNodeShutdown` and two new `KubeletConfiguration` options, `ShutdownGracePeriod` and `ShutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods`. 

With the feature gate enabled and the kubelet config options set, kubelet can delay a system shutdown by `ShutdownGracePeriod` and terminate pods gracefully prior to the node being shutdown.

Having read the KEP, I have only one real question.  If I have a pod that wants 5m of gracePeriod and it lands on a preemptible VM which can only ever deliver 30 seconds grace, should the scheduler not put it there?

IOW, do we need a node to declare an upper-bound for grace period that we can respect when scheduling?

@thockin, thanks for taking a look at the KEP and PR. 

Regarding the question you’re raising, this is a definitely a completely valid point -- the node doesn’t expose the "supported" grace period to the scheduler, so the scheduler isn’t able to take this into account.

My thoughts on this -- today during a node shutdown, gracePeriod on PodSpec is completely ignored by both scheduler and kubelet. There is no graceful node shutdown. This PR improves upon that situation as upon a shutdown with this feature enabled, the pod will get SOME gracePeriod to shutdown gracefully. As a result, I think the result is a net improvement over the current situation. 

Exposing the supported gracePeriod as part of the NodeSpec up to the scheduler, is something we should consider moving forward for this effort and bring on board scheduling SIG folks to get their thoughts. 

One thing that comes to mind though, is if the scheduler would suddenly start respecting gracePeriod supported by the node, it could be a breaking change for users. E.g. if my cluster is full of PVMs that support 30 seconds and my pod spec gracePeriod is 5 minutes, with new scheduler behavior, suddenly many pods will be unschedulable. That may or may not be a feature though :)

ACk that it can be integrated, but I do think we should come back to it.

This comment is really about the KEP and not your implementation - let me know if this thread should go in the issue instead.

First at a high level I think the KEP is well intentioned in trying to handle arbitrary causes of node reboot, but in practice most kubernetes admins (and node controllers like [the MCO](https://github.com/openshift/machine-config-operator/)) should be explicitly draining beforehand.   Let's be sure we interact well with that common case. 

Does `killPod` act as drain does and delete from the apiserver?  If not I think that's going to cause a lot of bugs.  Basically if we detect the unusual case of code not performing an explicit drain beforehand, then kubelet should fall back to a built in drain or so?

I was pointed at this KEP/PR from hitting https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/75482 - related to drain and daemonsets on node shutdown.

The "Update the Node's Ready condition to false, with the reason Node is shutting down" aspect of this makes total sense BTW - it seems like splitting that out as a small separate PR might be good to disentangle it from everything else.

Hi @cgwalters, thanks for your comments. A couple thoughts here:

> First at a high level I think the KEP is well intentioned in trying to handle arbitrary causes of node reboot, but in practice most kubernetes admins (and node controllers like the MCO) should be explicitly draining beforehand. Let's be sure we interact well with that common case.

Agree that most common pattern is to do explicit drain.

The node graceful shutdown implementation here  doesn't change that behavior in any way. Clusters admin (or controllers) should prefer to do an explicit drain if possible. However, an explicit drain is not always possible, for example for preemptible VMs or cases when for whatever reason a prior drain was not performed on the node -- that's the main goal here.      

> Does killPod act as drain does and delete from the apiserver? 

No, killPod does not remove the node from the apiserver. `killPod` simply kills the pod locally on the node. 

Drain login is not part of kubelet, it's a set of client side requests to api server: see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.19/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/drain/drain.go#L289

> If not I think that's going to cause a lot of bugs. Basically if we detect the unusual case of code not performing an explicit drain beforehand, then kubelet should fall back to a built in drain or so?

This is a pretty common case already, not all node removals are backed by a drain. For example, a node can randomly disconnect or fail. The [node lifecycle controller manager](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/nodelifecycle/node_lifecycle_controller.go) is responsible for managing lifecycle of node in this case, e.g. handle case of not receiving heartbeats from the node. 

As mentioned earlier, drain logic isn't part of kubelet. The end result of this implementation will have a similar effect though -- the node will be marked Unready and the pods will be gracefully terminated.  

If there's some issues due to a node being removed without a drain they'll continue to exist with or without this PR. If there's some known issue that you have in mind we should fix it :) 

> I was pointed at this KEP/PR from hitting #75482 - related to drain and daemonsets on node shutdown.

> The "Update the Node's Ready condition to false, with the reason Node is shutting down" aspect of this makes total sense BTW - it seems like splitting that out as a small separate PR might be good to disentangle it from everything else.

Updating the node ready condition to false and reason requires detecting the node shutdown in kubelet (integration with systemd inhibitors) which is the bulk of the PR here. As a result, I don't think it's possible to separate that out as it depends on kubelet being able to detect the shutdown in the first place.

> Updating the node ready condition to false and reason requires detecting the node shutdown in kubelet (integration with systemd inhibitors) which is the bulk of the PR here. 

Detecting shutdown is quite a different thing from inhibiting it (your patch).  Detecting shutdown is as easy as hooking up to `SIGTERM` - that model existed since pre-systemd era in Unix.  I think active inhibiting is really mostly a desktop/mobile case and had as a primary use case obsolete things like burning a CDROM where it physically couldn't be stopped.  

I think there's a far simpler approach, which is basically recommend people using kubelet via systemd unit to control `TimeoutStopSec=` if it's relevant to them.

Can you elaborate on the motivation for this work?  I can think of one example on e.g. on-premise bare metal where an administrator might want to decommission a node that's experiencing intermittent hardware errors.  In that case, the timeout for termination could be fairly long (an hour, a day even).  

In this case the `kubelet.service` might ship with a `TimeoutStopSec=24 hours` or even more.

In contrast the case of preemptible VMs (an important one): as noted this work doesn't do anything really to help it - the cloud provider is going to kill the VM regardless.  Our main goal here really should be to ensure that any "stateful" workload is gracefully deleted but other than that there's no reason to even kill the "system critical" pods because they'll die anyways when the VM goes down.


> This is a pretty common case already, not all node removals are backed by a drain.

I guess this hinges on whether one does in-place updates or not.  If so, then explicit drain is something like the 90%+ case.

>  For example, a node can randomly disconnect or fail. The node lifecycle controller manager is responsible for managing lifecycle of node in this case, e.g. handle case of not receiving heartbeats from the node.

Good point; so perhaps what I'm really arguing is that the node lifecycle controller should hook up to this "Ready=false, rebooting" flag and delete any remaining pods explicitly.  Or maybe there needs to be two separate flags, one for "reboot started" and one for "past the point of no return for reboot" and the lifecycle would only take action on the latter.


So to rephrase/summarize the above it feels like the bulk of this could be replaced with just bumping the `TimeoutStopSec`, but I do think there's important parts in the shutdown semantics and pod deletion to improve.
/milestone v1.20

Hi, @cgwalters

To clarify: The main goal of this KEP is to handle graceful pod termination during a node shutdown where the node is not explicitly drained beforehand. A clear example use case here is preemptible VMs. 

The `TimeoutStopSec=` does not address this use case, because it will prevent kubelet from shutting down, but does not result in graceful termination of pods on the node. During a node shutdown, systemd will still kill all of the underlying processes of container/pods running on the node without any graceful termination or respect to pod termination (preStopHooks, termination grace period, etc).
/lgtm
/lgtm

My notes from a real-time sync on this:

I came to be convinced the inhibitor is necessary because systemd will blast `SIGTERM` to everything and we need to avoid that.
We also can't generically hook onto `SIGTERM` because we want to support `systemctl restart kubelet` for development purposes at least, and that shouldn't flush all the containers.  General agreement this design is good as is for an alpha.

But we agreed that running services on the node is a key use case and ensuring the endpoint controller is reliably updated is important.  This led into discussion about pod deletion, and whether the kubelet sync loop should be doing that versus node lifecycle controller.    We'll revisit these types of things in the next update.
/approve

issue_context.title: Kubelet should handle node shutdown
issue_context.body:
<!-- Please only use this template for submitting enhancement requests -->

**What would you like to be added**:

Kubelet currently does not handle machine shutdown. Kubelet should be able to detect machine shutdown and gracefully terminate pods with attempt to respect pod's requested grace period.

**Why is this needed**:

Currently, when a machine is shutdown, Kubelet does not have any special handling to gracefully terminate pods. Machine shutdown can be a simple as `sudo shutdown now` or pressing the power key.

Some items to consider:

* Constrained machine shutdown time
    * In some cases, machines may or may not have a constrained time to shutdown. As a result, it's not always possible to respect a pod's requested grace period. 
       *  Certain cloud providers offer preemptive style VM's (e.g. [GCE Preemptible VM](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/preemptible) or [AWS EC2 Spot instances](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/using-spot-instances.html) that run at lower prices but can be terminated at any time with a fixed termination period (e.g. GCP PVMs offer 30 secs timeout, EC2 offers two-minutes). 
       * Some type of cloud provider integration of detecting preemption and specifying node termination period may be useful here 
       * Improving node shutdown would help experience of using preemptive style VMs with Kubernetes.

* Machine shutdown interference  (e.g. systemd)
    * In cases where kubelet is managed by systemd, systemd shutdown may interfere with kubelet. For example, during machine shutdown, systemd sends SIGTERM's to all processes on the VM (including all containers). This can potentially interfere with expected pod lifecycle (e.g. `preStopHooks` should be run before SIGTERM) [1]. There needs to be a way to ensure kubelet can mange lifecycle of pods during shutdown without systemd interference.   

[1] https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod/#termination-of-pods

Related to #66393, #30051

I commented in the KEP https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/2001/files#r565507971 but I don't think this is appropriate.  It forces an administrator deploying a system infrastructure pod to use one of these two priority classes to get this behavior, which means you can't create new priority classes for your critical infrastructure pods to control the order of eviction.  

Also, I expect all static pods to be covered by this logic, because it is impossible to drain a static pod correctly outside the kubelet (since kubelet controls the lifecycle, not an outside entity).

kube-apiserver depends on SDN (for aggregation and for webhooks). If both are implemented as static pods, and SDN is able to go through a LB to reach an apiserver on another node, how can we make sure SDN stays up longer than the static kube-apiserver pod?

is this lock needed to only call `processShutdownEvent ` once? If so, how is it working?

the `nodeShuttingDownMutex` is used to protect the `nodeShuttingDownNow` bool. The issue there is that the bool is read in `ShutdownStatus()` function and written in the go routine watching for shutdown events.

The   `ShutdownStatus` function is called by kubelet as part of the fetching the ready status in `pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go` in a seperate go routine. 

The issue is that the reading and writing to that bool can be done in two separate go routines, so to avoid data race I used the mutex.

what if somebody already have this file? Can there be more settings than just InhibitDelayMaxSec?
I'm confused. This setting is `InhibitDelayMaxSec ` and there is also a property `InhibitDelayMaxUSec`. Is it how everything designed?

`InhibitDelayMaxSec` is the name of the field that you configure by writing the logind file (see here https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/logind.conf.html). The config file only lets you set the InhibitDelay in second units. 

`InhibitDelayMaxUSec` is the name of the field when you query it via dbus. (documented here: https://www.freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/systemd/inhibit/). That should have the same value as configured in `InhibitDelayMaxSec` but it's measured in microseconds. 

In terms of why the config file is measured in seconds but the dbus setting is exposed as microseconds, I'm not sure, it's a bit confusing, but it's what logind does :)

what happens if this is acquired multiple times?

This is intended, the idea is that the user can cancel a pending shutdown. So the use case is that you schedule a shutdown in 5 minutes and then decide to cancel it. 

The recommend approach to deal with this case is on the systemd inhibit documentation: https://www.freedesktop.org/wiki/Software/systemd/inhibit/

It states:

> Here's the basic scheme for applications which need delay locks such as a web browser or office suite:
> 1. As you open a document, take the delay lock
> 2. As soon as you see PrepareForSleep(true), save your data, then release the lock
> 3. As soon as you see PrepareForSleep(false), take the delay lock again, continue as before.

That's kinda the same idea I'm trying to follow here:

1. When the shutdown manager starts up, we take the delay lock. 
2. When shutdown manager gets shutdown event (true), we evict all the pods and the release the lock. That's the job of the `processShutdownEvent()` function which is blocking call. Since it's a blocking call, we can guarantee that eventually when the `processShutdownEvent()` function returns, the inhibit lock will be released. 
3. If we ever get shutdown event false, we take the inhibit lock again.
so this may be `0` is duration was less than 1 second. Should this be checked on input so this config will be treated as invalid?
hmm, can you explain, I don't follow. `shutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods` can be zero, but I don't understand what you mean by "less than 1 second"...
`gracePeriodOverride` casts `float` number of seconds to `int64`. So if configuration (which is Duration) was configured with millisecond duration, this value will be `0`.

ah I see what you mean, nice catch. I added some validation as you suggested to ` pkg/kubelet/apis/config/validation/validation.go` to catch this case. 

Basically `ShutdownGracePeriod` and `ShutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods` must either be zero or if they're >= 0 they should be at least one second.
